question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Endocrine glands lack ducts and release hormones directly into the blood
options.B: Exocrine glands possess a rich network of fenestrated capillaries
options.C: Endocrine glands secrete substances exclusively onto the skin surface
options.D: Exocrine glands produce chemical messengers while endocrine glands do not

explanation: Think of endocrine glands as ductless delivery systems! Because they don't have tubes (ducts), they dump their hormones straight into the bloodstream to travel round the body. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why are the tiny blood vessels (capillaries) inside endocrine glands specially built?

options.A: They lack endothelial linings to let whole secretory cells escape
options.B: They have thick walls to withstand high pressure from hormone surges
options.C: They are fenestrated to allow quick entry of hormones into the bloodstream
options.D: They contain valves that prevent the backflow of endocrine secretions

explanation: Fenestrated just means 'having tiny windows or pores'! These little pores make the capillary walls super leaky in a good way, helping hormones hop straight into your blood in no time. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h1)

question: Where does the front part of the pituitary gland (anterior pituitary) come from during early development?

options.A: The bony depression of the sphenoid bone known as the sella turcica
options.B: Downward growth of neural tissue directly from the hypothalamus
options.C: An outpouching of the embryonic pharynx called Rathke's pouch
options.D: The mesodermal layer surrounding the developing brain structures

explanation: Rathke's pouch is a fascinating little pocket of tissue from the roof of the mouth that pinches off to form the glandular front part of your pituitary. Embryology can look tricky, but breaking it down makes it simple! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the main functional difference between the front (anterior) and back (posterior) lobes of the pituitary gland?

options.A: The anterior lobe responds to nervous signals, while the posterior lobe responds exclusively to chemical blood signals
options.B: The anterior lobe synthesizes its own hormones, while the posterior lobe only stores and releases them
options.C: The posterior lobe produces releasing factors, while the anterior lobe targets the hypothalamus
options.D: The posterior lobe contains glandular epithelial cords, while the anterior lobe is made entirely of neurons

explanation: Remember: the anterior pituitary is a factory that makes its own hormones, while the posterior pituitary is more like a warehouse that just stores and sends out what the brain (hypothalamus) made for it! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the job of the jelly-like substance (colloid) found inside your thyroid gland?

options.A: To provide a rigid structural framework supporting the larynx
options.B: To manufacture parathyroid hormone for the posterior glands
options.C: To store thyroid hormone precursors until they are ready for release
options.D: To produce calcitonin for the regulation of blood calcium levels

explanation: Colloid acts like a storage warehouse inside the thyroid follicles, holding onto hormone building blocks safely until your body gives the signal to release them. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h3)

question: How can you tell parathyroid tissue apart from thyroid tissue under a microscope?

options.A: Parathyroid glands contain large amounts of colloid material for hormone storage
options.B: Parathyroid tissue is arranged in dense cords and nests rather than hollow follicles
options.C: Parathyroid glands lack blood capillaries within their parenchymal clusters
options.D: Parathyroid tissue is lined exclusively by ciliated columnar epithelial cells

explanation: While the thyroid forms hollow ring-like 'follicles' filled with jelly, the parathyroid packs its cells into neat little clusters and cords surrounded by tiny blood vessels. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which layer of the outer adrenal gland (adrenal cortex) produces stress hormones like cortisol?
explanation: Think of the adrenal cortex layers from outside in as Salt, Sugar, Sex (Glomerulosa, Fasciculata, Reticularis). The middle layer, zona fasciculata, handles the 'sugar' hormones like cortisol to help you cope with stress! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h4)

question: What type of cells make up the inner part of the adrenal gland (adrenal medulla), and where do they come from?

options.A: C cells derived from the embryonic pharyngeal pouches
options.B: Chromaffin cells, which are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons
options.C: Epithelial cells arranged in hollow spherical follicles containing colloid
options.D: Follicular cells that synthesize and store mineralocorticoids

explanation: The adrenal medulla is unique! Its chromaffin cells are basically modified nerve cells that release adrenaline straight into your blood during a fight-or-flight moment. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary job of the alpha cells in the pancreas (Islets of Langerhans)?

options.A: Releasing digestive enzymes into pancreatic ducts
options.B: Producing insulin to lower circulating blood sugar
options.C: Synthesizing somatostatin to inhibit neighboring cells
options.D: Secreting glucagon to raise blood glucose levels

explanation: Easy way to remember: Alpha = 'A'lways brings sugar up (glucagon), while Beta cells bring blood sugar down with insulin. You've got this nursing concept down! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why do we call the pancreas a 'heterocrine' (or mixed) organ?

options.A: It releases secretions into both lymphatic vessels and blood capillaries
options.B: Its structure combines neural tissue with glandular epithelial cords
options.C: It produces two opposing hormones, insulin and glucagon, from beta cells
options.D: It contains both exocrine digestive tissue and endocrine hormone-producing islets

explanation: The pancreas wears two hats! It acts as an exocrine gland by sending digestive juices through ducts to your gut, and an endocrine gland by releasing hormones like insulin straight into your blood. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which hormone is produced by the pineal gland in your brain?
explanation: Melatonin is your body's natural clock keeper! Released by the pineal gland when it gets dark, it helps signal to your body that it's time to sleep. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h6)

question: What happens to the thymus gland as a person grows older?

options.A: It accumulates calcified deposits known as corpora arenacea
options.B: Its pinealocytes transform entirely into hormone-secreting neurons
options.C: It develops hollow colloid-filled follicles similar to the thyroid
options.D: It undergoes fatty involution and gradually shrinks in size

explanation: As we age, the active immune tissue in the thymus slowly gets replaced by fat cells—a natural process called involution. Nothing to worry about, it's just part of normal aging! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which hormone is released by special cells in the heart when the heart walls get stretched too much?
explanation: When your heart chambers are stretched by high blood volume, they release Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) to tell your kidneys to get rid of extra water and salt, helping lower your blood pressure. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h7)

question: How do hormone-producing cells in the Diffuse Neuroendocrine System (DNES) differ from traditional glands?

options.A: They consist exclusively of modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons derived from neural crest tissue
options.B: They possess specialized ducts that empty their chemical secretions directly into the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: They lack a blood supply entirely and rely purely on local nervous system stimulation for hormone distribution
options.D: Their hormone-producing cells are scattered singly among other mucosal cell types rather than clustered in a dedicated gland

explanation: Instead of sitting together in one organ (like the thyroid), DNES cells are scattered solo across places like your gut lining, quietly sending out local chemical signals. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h7)
